brief: Implement `simulate()`: given a synchronous sequential circuit of logic gates and flip-flops, simulate every random stimulus cycle by cycle from an all-zero state and fold the primary outputs into a 64-bit digest. Performance inputs have 500,000 gates, 8,192 flip-flops, 4,096 stimuli and 512 cycles each.

ul: The 9 performance inputs cover 3 circuit classes, 3 each; inputs, expected outputs, the compiled baseline reference.exe and a checker come with the task. The checker interleaves 3 runs each of the baseline and submission and takes each median; official scoring also remeasures both in the same evaluation. The baseline source code is not public.
Digests must match the expected output bit for bit, with no tolerance; 7 more correctness inputs stay hidden, and even tiny circuits must come out right.
CPU only: the C++ standard library, OpenMP, the Windows API, compiler built-ins and instruction intrinsics; no GPU and no other third-party libraries.
Digests must be computed by `simulate()` from the circuit passed in, never built in; the graded process is limited to the 8 performance cores.

points: **Bit-level parallelism**: pack many independent stimuli into 64-bit words and AVX2 vectors and compute them together.
**Circuit preprocessing**: gates are not given in dependency order; sorting, simplification and layout decide how fast evaluation is.
**Threads and caches**: with many stimuli and large circuits, batching, layout and division of work set the ceiling.
**Tuning per class**: the 3 classes, deep chains, array multipliers and register files, differ in topology, and strategy can be chosen per class.
scoring: **Scored per input**: each of the 9 performance inputs gets a speedup s = baseline time ÷ solution time, looked up on a log-scale anchor table, 0 at 0.1× or less; deep chains and array multipliers (inputs 1–6) use the table with full marks from 12×, while register files (inputs 7–9) use the table with full marks from 8×; an input that fails to run scores 0.

**Correctness factor**: the average over the 9 inputs is multiplied by the share of the 7 correctness inputs passed. Performance is scored only on these 9 inputs; the 7 hidden correctness inputs are not timed, and other circuits only need correct results.

**Timed side by side**: the baseline is a general optimized solution written by the task setter; it and the solution each run 3 times in the same evaluation under the same conditions, taking the median.
**Rules come first**: a compile failure or a broken rule, such as using the GPU or writing precomputed digests into the code, scores 0 for the whole task.
